This bill would reintroduce three measures from the 2015 Budget that were removed from an earlier bill in June 2015.

It would cut from two weeks to six weeks the period that age pension and certain other payment recipients receive their full basic rate while overseas, then adjust payments based on Australian working life residence.

The bill would also freeze income free areas for working age allowances and student payments from 1 July 2016 and 1 January 2016 respectively, and cease the pensioner education supplement from 1 January 2016.
Reduces the portability period for age pension and some other payments from two weeks to six weeks.
Freezes income free areas for working age allowances and student payments for three years.
Ends the pensioner education supplement from 1 January 2016.
Age pension recipients and a small number of people on other payments with unlimited portability, as well as recipients of working age allowances and student payments.
Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015 - Second Reading - Agree with the bill's main idea

The speaker argued that the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015 is necessary to address a $100 million daily interest bill on debt accrued under the previous Labor government, which left $191 billion in deficits and $123 billion in projected deficits. The speaker stated that the bill does not cut pensions for those who have lived in Australia for 35 years, but introduces a six-week overseas portability limit with proportional reductions for shorter residency, and saves $500 million by removing outdated education supplements.

The speaker argued the government unfairly targets low-income Australians, pensioners, and unemployed youth with budget cuts while protecting wealthy superannuants and multinationals avoiding tax. Specific measures criticised include changing overseas pension payments, abolishing the pensioner education supplement, and freezing income-free areas for working-age allowances, which the speaker said would push more people into poverty, citing 30% of Bendigo’s electorate surviving on under $600 per week.

The speaker argued that the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015 is essential for Australia's long-term economic health, citing Labor's $191 billion in deficits and a projected $667 billion deficit without policy change.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015, arguing it unfairly targets vulnerable Australians, particularly pensioners, by cutting overseas pension payments after six weeks, abolishing the pensioner education supplement and education entry payment, and pausing indexation. They also criticised the government for doubling the deficit and for its record on pensioner cuts since 2013.

Opposition members opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015, which included measures affecting pensioners travelling overseas, cuts to the pensioner education supplement and education entry payment, and changes to indexation.

The speaker argued that the budget is in desperate need of repair, citing nine consecutive years of deficits, daily borrowing of $100 million, and $14 billion in annual interest payments, and quoted former Labor Prime Minister Paul Keating in support of spending cuts.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015, arguing it unfairly cuts the overseas pension payment period from 26 weeks to six weeks and abolishes the pensioner education supplement and education entry payment. Labor will not support the bill.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015, arguing it targets older Australians and vulnerable people, and highlighted three measures: reducing overseas pension portability from 26 to 6 weeks, abolishing the pensioner education supplement affecting 41,300 people (mostly women), and abolishing the education entry payment affecting 87,000 people.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015, arguing it would cut age pension payments for migrants who travel overseas for more than six weeks, creating a discriminatory system that saves $168.4 million over four years at the expense of vulnerable pensioners.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015, arguing it unfairly targets vulnerable groups. The bill would reduce pension portability for overseas visits from 26 weeks to six weeks for those with fewer than 35 years of Australian work history, abolish the $208 education entry payment for 87,000 recipients, and cut the pensioner education supplement of $31–$61 per fortnight for 41,130 people, three-quarters of whom are women.

The MP opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015, arguing it unfairly cuts $579 million from pensioners and students, including abolishing the pensioner education supplement and education entry payment, and restricting overseas pension portability to six weeks for those who have lived in Australia less than 35 years. The MP also cited broader government policies—such as pension asset-test changes, increased pension age, and possible GST rises—as disproportionately hitting low- and middle-income Australians.

The government argued that reducing the portability period for age pension payments overseas from 26 weeks to six weeks, saving $168 million, is necessary for budget repair and fairness, as Australia is one of few nations paying a non-contributory pension abroad indefinitely. The bill also reintroduces measures to cease the pensioner education supplement and education entry payment, and freeze indexation of income-free areas for three years.

The majority agreed with the main idea of the bill. In parliamentary jargon, they agreed to give the bill a [second reading](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). This means that the House can now discuss the bill in more detail. ### Bill's main idea The main idea of the bill is to undo some of the measures that haven't yet begun but were introduced under the previous Labor Government's 2013-14 Budget. That is, it repeals all the parts of the [Clean Energy (Income Tax Rates Amendments) Act 2011](https://www.comlaw.gov.au/Details/C2011A00150) and the [Clean Energy (Tax Laws Amendments) Act 2011](https://www.comlaw.gov.au/Details/C2011A00159) that were meant to begin at a future date. The bill doesn't repeal any parts of those two Acts that are already in operation. ### What exactly does the bill do? According to the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1415a/15bd026), the bill will: * "*repeal an increase in the nominal tax-free threshold from $18,200 in 2014–15 to $19,400 in 2015–16* * *maintain the second personal marginal tax rate at 32.5 per cent rather than increase it to 33 per cent from 2015–16* * *maintain the maximum value of the low income tax offset (**LITO**) at $445 rather than change the maximum value of the LITO to $300 from 2015–16 and* * *maintain the threshold below which a person may receive LITO at a taxable income of $66,667 and the withdrawal rate at 1.5 per cent, rather than the income threshold increasing to $67,000 and the withdrawal rate falling to 1 per cent from 2015–16.*"

Labor will oppose the bill at second reading but support it after government amendments remove the efficiency dividend and interest charge measures, while backing the conversion of student start-up scholarships to income-contingent loans and the removal of the HECS-HELP discount and voluntary repayment bonus, yielding $1.1 billion in budget savings.

The speaker supported converting student start-up scholarships into income-contingent loans (saving $920 million) and removing the HECS-HELP upfront payment discount and voluntary repayment bonus (saving $200 million), but opposed the efficiency dividend for higher education funding and imposing interest charges on debts like Abstudy and Austudy. The speaker argued these measures were originally proposed to fund the Gonski needs-based school funding model, which the government cut by $28 billion, and that the bill’s other measures represent an ideological attack on education, including introducing $100,000 university degrees.

The speaker argued that the Turnbull-Truss coalition government is a superior financial manager compared to the previous Labor government, citing a reduction in the budget deficit from $48 billion to $7 billion, a drop in unemployment from 6.2% to 5.9%, and 231,702 new jobs created. The speaker supported the Labor 2013-14 Budget Savings (Measures No. 2) Bill 2015, which includes an efficiency dividend for higher education grants and interest charges on unpaid Centrelink debts, and criticized Labor for wasteful spending and a lack of infrastructure projects in Western Australia.

The speech criticised the bill for adding $6,000 in average student debt and proposed fairer revenue measures, including ending the $2 billion diesel fuel rebate for miners, winding back superannuation tax concessions, or introducing a millionaire’s tax rate.

The speaker argued that Labor's 2013-14 Budget Savings Bill is needed to address Labor's $52 billion budget black hole, and criticised the Greens and Labor for blocking $17.2 billion in savings measures, including $2.1 billion in changes to student start-up scholarships and $1.2 billion in higher education efficiency dividends.

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2015-11-30.142.2) that the [*Social Services Legislation Amendment (Family Payments Structural Reform and Participation Measures) Bill 2015*](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5557) be read a first time. Passing this motion means that the bills can be introduced into the Senate. [According to The Parliament](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5557#sched), this bill: > Amends the [A New Tax System (Family Assistance) Act 1999](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsaa1999357/) to restructure family tax benefit Part B by removing the benefit for couple families (other than grandparents or great-grandparents) with a youngest child 13 years of age or over. According to [Odgers’ Australian Senate Practice](http://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Senate/Powers_practice_n_procedures/odgers13?file=chapter12§ion=05), “the first reading is normally passed without opposition and is regarded as a purely formal stage”. That the Senate [divided to vote on this motion, rather than passing it “on the voices”](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/help/faq#division-occur), suggests that the [amendments](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Famend%2Fr5557_amend_1024de59-f06b-4722-9ffe-f189a44de518%22;rec=0) to the [*A New Tax System (Family Assistance) Act 1999*](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsaa1999357/) included in this bill were controversial.

The speaker argued that Labor has defeated proposed cuts to family payments worth $8.5 billion and then $4.8 billion, protecting 1.6 million families and three million children from losing up to $4,700 per year for a single-parent household. They demanded the Turnbull government abandon further cuts and release departmental modelling on the impacts.

The speaker opposed the bill, arguing it cuts $4.06 billion from family tax benefit supplements affecting 1.5 million families, including 600,000 single-parent families. He criticised the government’s childcare package as an unsubstantiated false trade-off and said the $380 million newborn payment was a political arrangement with the National Party.

The speaker argued that the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Family Payments Structural Reform and Participation Measures) Bill 2015 is necessary to simplify a complex welfare system that cost $145 billion annually, with spending growing 43% in a decade and $5 billion potentially lost to rorts, and criticised the opposition for blocking reforms.

Labor successfully opposed cuts to family tax benefits, protecting 1.6 million families and 3 million children from losing up to $4,700 per year, but the schoolkids bonus cuts remain and the government should clarify its future plans.

The speaker argued the bill is necessary for fiscal sustainability and to fund programs like the Nanny Pilot Program, and criticised Labor for not addressing how to pay for welfare spending, noting that nearly half the population are net noncontributors and that the schoolkids bonus is funded by borrowed money.

The speaker argued that the Turnbull-Abbott government repeatedly targets vulnerable Australians for budget savings instead of addressing high-end superannuation, and supported amendments to the Family Payments bill on family tax benefit part B changes, which save $1.4 billion over four years, while warning that the government may reintroduce more draconian measures. They criticised the member for Parkes for implying that welfare recipients squander payments, and noted that 140,000 single parents and 76,000 couples would lose family tax benefit part A under the original bill.

The speaker argued that the bill would cut family tax benefits for 1.5 million families, including 650,000 single parents and 500,000 on incomes under $51,000, while increasing payments for 140,000 families with children under one. They welcomed government amendments but criticised the lack of detail on a linked childcare package and accused the government of unfairness toward low-income families.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Family Payments Structural Reform and Participation Measures) Bill 2015, arguing it unfairly cut family payments to low- and middle-income families, particularly in disadvantaged electorates like Throsby, where over 10,500 families receive Family Tax Benefit Part A and 9,400 receive Part B, with households in suburbs like Berkeley and Warrawong facing losses of $500–$550 annually. He cited NATSEM and Jesuit Social Services reports showing the coalition's budgets hit the poorest hardest while benefiting high-income families.

The government argued for the Social Services Legislation Amendment bill to fund childcare reform, claiming Labor reduced a $4.7 billion childcare package to $525 million. The speaker announced changes to Family Tax Benefit B eligibility and a $3.5 billion Jobs for Families package, including a nanny pilot program for 10,000 children.

The government will amend the bill to only include ending Family Tax Benefit Part B for couple families when the youngest child turns 13, a measure the opposition agreed to, while other savings—including phasing out end-of-year supplements worth $4.1 billion—will be reintroduced separately to fund $3.5 billion in childcare reforms and budget repair.

Tax and Superannuation Laws Amendment (Better Targeting the Income Tax Transparency Laws) Bill 2015 - Second Reading - Agree with the bill's main idea

Labor opposed the Tax and Superannuation Laws Amendment (Better Targeting the Income Tax Transparency Laws) Bill 2015, arguing it would gut transparency for the roughly 2,000 firms earning over $100 million and exempt all private firms, and moved an amendment to block the bill. The party promoted its own $7.2 billion multinational tax package as an alternative, referencing Wayne Swan and David Bradbury's 2013 reforms.

The speaker opposed the Tax and Superannuation Laws Amendment (Better Targeting the Income Tax Transparency Laws) Bill 2015, arguing it would exempt Australian-owned private companies from disclosure and normalise tax avoidance. They criticised BHP Billiton and Rio Tinto for using Singapore marketing hubs to shift profits and avoid paying fair tax in Australia, citing $5.7 billion and $4.5 billion in profits booked in Singapore respectively, with effective tax rates well below the corporate average.

The speaker opposed the Tax and Superannuation Laws Amendment (Better Targeting the Income Tax Transparency Laws) Bill 2015, arguing it punishes successful private companies and invades their privacy, and supported an amendment by the member for Fraser.
The Bill reduces the number of employees required for a company's tax information to be made public from 250 to 100, aiming to increase transparency of large private companies' tax practices.

The speaker opposed the bill, arguing it would reduce tax transparency by exempting private companies from publishing tax information, and criticised the government for cutting 4,700 ATO staff and reopening $1.1 billion in tax loopholes. They promoted Labor's alternative policy to raise over $500 million annually through measures including a worldwide gearing ratio and increased ATO compliance.

The bill repeals a Labor-era requirement for private companies with turnover over $100 million to publicly disclose tax records, arguing it protects privacy, prevents commercial exploitation, and encourages entrepreneurial activity, while contrasting coalition achievements like repealing carbon and mining taxes with Labor’s record.

The speaker argued that the government's tax transparency bill weakens Labor's legislation and fails to crack down on multinational tax avoidance, which costs Australia billions. They cited specific figures: the government's tax avoidance effort is worth only $30 million over four years compared to Labor's $1.9 billion plan, and 29% of ASX 200 companies pay an effective tax rate of 10% or less, resulting in an estimated $8.4 billion annual revenue loss.

The speaker argued that exempting Australian-owned private companies from publishing tax information is necessary to protect their commercial confidentiality and market security, citing risks to intellectual property and profit margins. They criticised Labor for not applying similar transparency to unions and emphasised the coalition’s commitment to implementing OECD anti-tax avoidance measures like country-by-country reporting.

The bill exempts Australian-owned private companies from public tax disclosure requirements, arguing the measure protects their privacy and competitiveness while preserving the ATO's enforcement powers. The government also announced broader actions against multinational tax avoidance, including new anti-avoidance rules, GST on foreign digital services, and doubled penalties for large companies using profit-shifting schemes.
Tax and Superannuation Laws Amendment (Better Targeting the Income Tax Transparency Laws) Act 2015

Brendan O'Connor As I was saying before this debate was moved to another part of business for the parliament, this bill, the Construction Industry (Protecting Witnesses) Bill, is to be opposed by the opposition because it is about whether the sunset provision should continue. It is the view of the opposition—implicit in the sunset clause—that it is incumbent upon the government to establish whether such a provision should continue. In other words, the onus is on the government to explain why they believe there is sufficient evidence to warrant the extension of this provision. And we would argue—given that there has been no review undertaken by the government in this matter—that the sunset provision should take effect, and that therefore the effect of the provision should lapse, because of the government's failure to review this matter. It is also interesting to note that, of course, this provision relates to the Australian Building and Construction Commission. It relates to the efforts by this government to reinstate such a commission—which we would argue is an overreach, excessive, and in breach of international human rights conventions—and, whilst the government still has that intention, it is interesting to note that in the budget documents of yesterday, in the strategic directions under this portfolio, it is no longer a priority in the way it was outlined in last year's budget. In last year's budget, there was a priority for the establishment of the Australian Building and Construction Commission. And yet that is no longer the case; it has been relegated down the order in the budget, which I think reflects the fact that the minister and indeed the government understand that they do not have the support of the parliament to proceed with their efforts to re-establish the Australian Building and Construction Commission. The Construction Industry Amendment (Protecting Witnesses) Bill 2015 extends for two years the compulsory powers of Fair Work Building and Construction to compel witness testimony, preventing their expiry on 1 June 2015, in order to combat unlawful conduct, thuggery and intimidation in the construction industry.

The speaker opposed the Construction Industry Amendment (Protecting Witnesses) Bill 2015, arguing the government had not conducted the required review of the sunset clause on coercive powers, which were used only four times in 2013–14, and called for a review instead of extension.

The Construction Industry Amendment (Protecting Witnesses) Bill 2015 extends compulsory examination powers of Fair Work Building and Construction beyond 1 June 2015 to prevent compromising current investigations, pending Senate re-establishment of the Australian Building and Construction Commission. The speaker argued that Labor originally created these powers under Prime Minister Gillard, and that the CFMEU and ETU oppose them despite a culture of intimidation in the industry, citing the Royal Commission into Trade Union Governance and Corruption.
Customs Tariff Amendment (China-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2015

The speaker concluded the debate on the Customs Tariff Amendment (China-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2015, urging its passage to implement the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement (ChAFTA). He highlighted benefits including tariff eliminations on resources, energy, and agriculture, new market access for services, and a raised investment screening threshold for private Chinese investors, citing support from business groups and projecting job growth in sectors like dairy and financial services.

The speaker introduced the enabling legislation for the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement, calling it the highest quality and most liberalising trade deal China has done with any developed country and the best for Australia in goods, services and investment, and argued that only two modest customs bills are needed with no changes to migration laws, contrary to claims by the CFMEU and ETU.

The Customs Tariff Amendment (China-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2015 was moved for a second reading, proposing duty-free access for certain Chinese-originating goods upon entry into force, preferential tariff rates phased to zero over three or five years for items including plastics, rubber, paper, textiles, clothing, footwear, base metals, and excise-equivalent duties on alcohol, tobacco, and petroleum products.
